IDM 216 — Mobile UX Case Study

Pete's Little
Lunchbox

Role UX Designer + Front-End Coder
Team 5 Wheel Drive (5 members)
Platform Mobile Web App
Duration 10 Weeks/Winter Quarter 2026
01 — Overview

A mobile ordering experience built for the lunch rush.

Pete's Little Lunchbox is a real food truck on Drexel's campus that needed a mobile web app where customers can browse the menu, place an order, and get a clear order number to show at the window. My team, 5 Wheel Drive, started with a design from a previous term and built on it, using usability testing to shape it into a more polished final product.

I worked across the whole UX process. I refined the personas and user journeys we inherited, designing and iterating on screens in Figma, running usability tests, and even contributing to some front-end microinteractions in CodePen. A lot of our key decisions came directly from what users told us and design improvements from last quarter's design — people needed an easier way to get back to their order details, and the order number had to be big and obvious so they could just show it at the window without thinking twice.

Project Type

Iterative redesign of an existing mobile food-ordering app

My Role

UX Designer — UI screens, personas, journeys, usability testing + some front-end

Key Outcome

Two rounds of usability testing drove meaningful, user-validated design changes

Team

5 members across design, project management, and front/back-end development

02 — Context & Challenge

Building on someone else's foundation.

Background

Pete's Little Lunchbox is an existing food truck with a loyal customer base. The course project challenged teams to design and build a functional mobile ordering app, based on a design from last term, for a real client scenario. Our team's version of this project was a continuation of work begun by a previous team the prior term. This meant we inherited wireframes, screen layouts, and user research artifacts that needed to be reviewed, validated, and evolved rather than replaced entirely.

The Problem

Food truck customers often deal with a pretty disjointed ordering experience. Customers were waiting in line, trying to remember what they ordered, and didn't have a clear order number to use at a busy window. The app needed to smooth out that whole flow — from browsing the menu to placing an order to getting a confirmation that actually works in a real-world setting.

Inheriting a prior team's work introduced an additional layer of challenge. We had to assess what was worth keeping, what needed refinement, and what the previous design had missed — all without the benefit of having been there to understand the original decisions.

Goals & Objectives

Success for this project was defined by three things:

Usability: Users can navigate from the home screen to placing a completed order without confusion or dead ends.

Real-world utility: The order confirmation screen must be immediately legible when a customer shows it at a food truck window.

Iterative improvement: Design decisions between Alpha and Beta must be visibly driven by usability testing data, not assumptions.

03 — Process & Insight

From inherited foundations to tested solutions.

1

Reviewing & Adapting Inherited Work

Rather than discard the prior team's efforts, I began by auditing their Figma screens, user personas, and journey map with fresh eyes. I updated the personas and journey map to better reflect the context of our term and to align with what our team understood about the app's core use cases. Most screens were carried forward with minor adjustments; others were flagged for redesign based on early team consensus before any testing began.

Screenshot of last quarter's team's Figma file.

2

User Journey Map

Working from the prior team's foundation, I built out a detailed user journey map centered on our primary persona, Karen T. — a busy Drexel student squeezing in a quick meal between classes. The map traces her experience across six stages: rushing out without breakfast, spotting the truck, reading the menu, placing her order, waiting, and finally paying. For each stage I mapped her goals, actions, thoughts, pain points, and emotional state, then identified opportunities where the app could meaningfully reduce friction — from pre-ordering, to a clearer menu layout, to a prominent order number system. This map became the backbone of our design priorities throughout the project.

User Journey Map.

3

UI Design — Alpha Screens

I adjusted the mobile interface screens in Figma for the Alpha phase, focusing on the critical path: home → item selection → cart → order confirmation. All screens were designed mobile-first. I ensured interactive elements (buttons, checkboxes, menus) were visually distinct and touch-friendly, and that the navigation between all screens was clearly signed and included a confirmation screen centered on a large, legible order number.

I also built the initial Figma prototype used for usability testing, linking screens together to simulate the ordering flow so testers could navigate it as they would a real app. Alongside this, I contributed to scoping decisions with the team given that we had just 10 weeks to deliver a fully functional web app, we had to be deliberate about what to cut. I helped identify features and options that were lower priority or too complex to implement cleanly in the time available, so the team could focus on getting the core experience right rather than spreading too thin.

4

Usability Testing — Round One (Alpha)

I wrote the usability testing script for the Alpha phase, focusing on two main areas: navigability (can users find what they need without help?) and ease of flow (can they move through the app smoothly without getting stuck?). We ran the test over Zoom, with the script set up in a Google Form. My teammate Saffron and I switched between being the interviewer and the notetaker, while the participant shared their screen and walked through the prototype while sharing their thoughts aloud.

After the first round of testing, it became clear that the menu in the prototype was pretty predictable, so users could follow instructions almost on autopilot instead of actually searching for things. Because of that, we didn't get a fully accurate read on true navigability.

I addressed this in the Beta round, which followed the same general format but used the coded web app instead of the Figma prototype. This made the experience feel more real and gave us better insight into how users actually move through the product.

Screenshot of the intro to the Alpha usability testing script.

Alpha Usability Test Results — 6 responses

Key Insights:

Users couldn't find their way back to their order details after the confirmation screen — there was no intuitive return path, which would be a real problem if a customer needed to double-check their items.

The order number was too small for practical use at the truck window. In a real-world scenario, a user would need to hold up their phone to a staff member — a small number buried in a confirmation layout simply doesn't work.

5

UI Iteration — Beta Screens

Based on the Alpha findings, my team and I made two primary design changes for Beta. First, we added a clear navigation path back to the order summary from the confirmation screen, giving users confidence that their order was saved and reviewable. Second, we redesigned the order confirmation screen so the order number dominates the full screen, with large type and high contrast, making it unmistakably easy to show at the window. Lastly, users wanted to be able to browse the menu and build their order before being asked to sign in or create an account. We implemented this in Beta — users were able to scroll the full menu and curate their order freely, and are only prompted to add a phone number at the checkout screen for order update purposes. This removed a friction point that could have caused drop-off before users even committed to ordering.

I also shuffled item placement in the menu layout in the coded web app prototype for the Beta usability test, so that testers would need to actually look for items rather than follow a predictable pattern, thus producing more honest navigability data.

Screenshot of the intro page of the Beta Usability Testing script.

6

Front-End Contributions

My primary role was UX Design, but I also contributed to the front-end layer. I built microinteraction prototypes in CodePen — small, focused demos exploring hover states, button feedback, and transition animations — which the team could reference and adapt when coding the final application. This was a supporting role; our two dedicated front-end developers led the implementation work.

7

Front-End Contributions

While front-end development was primarily led by our two dedicated coders, I contributed to microinteraction prototypes in CodePen — specifically supporting button state feedback and some interactive navigation elements. Given that one of our coders had a very specific and well-developed coding style (particularly on the back end), she preferred to lead the structural build to maintain consistency. My front-end involvement was a supporting one, stepping in where capacity was needed rather than owning a dedicated code stream.

04 — The Solution

A food truck app that works the way the lunch rush does.

The final product is a mobile web app that guides users through a fast, intuitive ordering flow — landing on a warm, branded home screen, moving through a scannable menu with clearly actionable item cards, building a cart, and arriving at an order confirmation screen designed entirely around one job: showing your number at the window.

Final screens: splash page, menu, and order confirmation.

Defining Features

✦

Full-Screen Order Number

The most significant UX decision in the project. The confirmation screen was redesigned so the order number fills the majority of the screen in bold, high-contrast type. No squinting, no hunting — just a number that works in daylight, across a counter, from an arm's length away.

✦

Return Path to Order Details

After placing an order, users can navigate back to their order summary at any point. This addresses a real anxiety in the food truck context: "Wait, did I actually order the right thing?" The return path gives users confidence without requiring them to start over.

✦

Streamlined Critical Path

The navigation structure was kept deliberately linear and low-friction — home, menu, cart, confirmation — with clear back navigation and consistent button placement throughout. Every interactive element was styled to be immediately recognizable as tappable, with sufficient size and contrast for outdoor mobile use.

05 — Results

Tested twice. Improved each time.

The project was a success in its primary goal: delivering a functional, tested, user-validated mobile ordering experience for Pete's Little Lunchbox. Both rounds of usability testing produced actionable findings, and the Beta design directly reflected those changes — a clear demonstration of a working iterative design process.

What Worked Well

The team's use of MS Teams Planner and a centralized wiki was a genuine strength. Task ownership was clear, progress was visible, and communication didn't fall through the cracks — especially important for a five-person team balancing dual roles. The iterative testing structure (Alpha → Beta → Final) gave us a real mechanism to improve the design based on evidence rather than instinct.

Lessons Learned

Start coding collaboration earlier. One of our primary coders found it easier to build the structure independently due to her distinct coding style — which produced clean, consistent output, but meant the rest of us were less involved in the build than intended. Starting that collaboration earlier, with time to align on conventions, would have distributed the workload more evenly and reduced end-of-project pressure.

Design test prototypes to require real navigation. The Alpha prototype made it too easy for users to follow instructions without genuinely exploring the interface. Introducing deliberate unpredictability into the prototype layout — shuffling items, removing obvious signposts — produces far more honest usability data. We corrected this for Beta and it showed in the quality of findings.

Inherited work requires active re-ownership. Taking over a prior team's designs isn't passive, it requires interrogating every decision, not just carrying work forward unchanged. Asking "why was this designed this way?" before the first test saved us from carrying forward assumptions that didn't hold up under scrutiny.
